newsitem.title: USA: Alaska Supreme Court strikes mine permits.
newsitem.headline: Alaska Supreme Court strikes mine permits.

text.p: Juneau city officials acted improperly when they approved permits that would allow Echo Bay Mines to construct its Alaska-Juneau gold mine, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled on Friday.
The Juneau Planning Commission erred in its 1993 approval, which was subject to a series of yet-to-be-met conditions, the court ruled.

"If allowed to use such phasing in response to defects in mining applications, the Commission could grant approval to any permit application no matter how deficient it is," Justice Warren Matthews said in the unanimous decision.
That would make the Juneau planning code "virtually meaningless" and would make decisions by the commission "effectively unreviewable," Matthews wrote.
The Supreme Court ordered the Juneau Assembly and planning commission to revoke the permits.
The ruling was a victory for the Thane Neighborhood Association and Alaskans for Juneau, two community groups that have opposed construction of the mine.
The groups had sued the City and Borough of Juneau over the mine permit, the first issued under the city's 1989 mining ordinance.

Echo Bay, which intervened on behalf of the city and borough, will not be adversely affected because it has already dramatically changed its mine plan and will submit new permit applications to state, federal and local governments.
"We see a silver lining in it. To us, it clarifies, before we go back to this process, what needs to be done," said David Stone, spokesman for Echo Bay's Alaska division.

The proposed mine is four miles from downtown Juneau. It would re-open the old Alaska-Juneau mine, which operated during the early part of the century and produced more than 3 million ounces of gold before it closed during the Second World War.

Under the plan submitted in 1993, Echo Bay was seeking to build a 332-foot (100 metre) high tailings dam with the mine's waste rock in Sheep Creek Valley, a popular recreation area. Excess water from the tailings pond would have been discharged into Juneau's Gastineau Channel.
The tailings and wastewater disposal plan have been the most controversial elements of Echo Bay's mine proposal.
After the Environmental Protection Agency panned the company's development plan late last year, Echo Bay announced it would redesign the project.
The new mine plan eliminates the tailings dam entirely and relies on marine disposal of the waste rock. EPA has yet to approve that proposal.
The new mine plan also eliminates the use of cyanide to process gold.
